questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain the impeachment threshold and its purpose.
questions.stem: Explain in your own words what the impeachment threshold is, why it is set high, and what a lower threshold would change.

answer.exemplar: The impeachment threshold is the level of support required before the assembly may begin proceedings to remove a person from office; in our guild it is two thirds of all the members present, not a simple majority. It is set high because the power to impeach is the most severe the assembly holds and because a low threshold would let a temporary coalition of grievances remove an official on a wave of anger. A lower threshold would make the office less secure, would chill independent judgement by officials who spend more time protecting themselves than doing the work, and would turn ordinary political disputes into campaigns for dismissal.

questions.explanation: The threshold is the support needed to begin removal proceedings, set high because the power is severe and a low bar makes offices insecure. The argument for a simple majority ignores temporary coalitions.
questions.hint: It is the bar for starting proceedings.

questions.explanation: The rules set the complaint threshold first, and only a complaint carrying a tenth of members justifies a committee. Starting at the debate or the decision skips the gate the rules place first.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Weigh the value and risk of a ceremonial head.
questions.stem: Weigh what the ceremonial head of state contributes that an elected speaker could not, and set out the risk in the role at the same time.

answer.exemplar: A ceremonial head contributes two things an elected speaker cannot. The first is a symbol of continuity that stands outside party politics, so that when the council is deadlocked the country still has a lawful figure to whom the business of state can be addressed and who can sign the decrees that keep the machinery running. The second is the capacity for a word of encouragement or restraint at moments when the council cannot find agreement, which a speaker bound by the proceedings of the chamber could never offer. The risk lies in the same ambiguity. A ceremonial head who stays silent may become a mere decoration, and one who speaks too freely becomes an unelected rival to the council, whose advice is heard but never accountable to the voters.

questions.explanation: The ceremonial head gives continuity outside party politics, but silence risks an empty role and speech risks an unelected rival. The view that the role should go ignores both contributions.
questions.hint: Continuity outside party, but speak with care.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Compare a qualified appropriation with an ordinary one.
questions.stem: Describe how a qualified appropriation differs from an ordinary one, and explain why the council might prefer the qualified form.

answer.exemplar: An ordinary appropriation authorises a payment outright once it is agreed. A qualified appropriation authorises it subject to a condition, so the money is released only when something specified has happened or been verified, and if the condition is not met the authority to spend simply does not arise. The council may prefer the qualified form because it keeps the decision with the council at the point when the condition is tested, rather than handing the officer an unconditional blank cheque at the outset. The qualification can be a certificate from an inspector, a report to the chamber before the second instalment, or a demonstration that the goods were delivered as ordered. The cost of the form is delay and administrative work, and the condition must be drafted precisely enough to be applied.

questions.explanation: A qualified appropriation ties money release to a condition, so the council keeps a decision when the condition is tested. The view that qualification merely delays payment ignores that it can prevent payment.
questions.hint: Money follows a condition, not just a vote.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Weigh the case for a pardon power.
questions.stem: Weigh the case for retaining a pardon power at all, and give a balanced conclusion about how it should be used.

answer.exemplar: The case for retaining pardon is that no legal system is flawless. Without it, a mistaken conviction cannot be undone by the body that committed the error, and a person who has served years for a crime later proved to have been committed by another must remain in prison. A narrow power of mercy is also how a state expresses that the sentence imposed was too severe in the particular case, which keeps punishment in proportion. The case against is that mercy unaccounted for is arbitrary, that pardons are often granted to those with powerful friends, and that the presence of the power invites the executive to bargain with the courts. The conclusion is to keep a narrow power, exercised on a published recommendation from the courts, recorded with reasons, and applied at a rate visible to the legislature.

questions.explanation: Pardon corrects errors nothing else reaches, but only with published reasons and narrow scope, otherwise it is bargaining. The position that mercy should never exist ignores that finality can be injustice.
questions.hint: Keep it narrow, reasoned and visible.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish a public inquiry from a select committee.
questions.stem: Explain why a public committee of inquiry differs from an ordinary select committee in the way it is used.

answer.exemplar: A select committee examines one subject quietly and reports to the chamber, and its work is usually limited to what the chamber itself has referred to it. A public committee of inquiry is convened to establish the facts of a matter of public concern, and its distinguishing features are openness, compulsion and publication. It sits in public, so the public can watch and the witnesses perform before a public gallery; it can require the attendance of persons and the production of documents, so that a witness cannot simply decline; and it publishes its evidence and its findings, so that the account survives the political weather of the day. These features make the inquiry an instrument of public reassurance as well as of discovery, because the public learns not only what happened but that it was examined by a body which could not be managed by the parties involved.

questions.explanation: A public inquiry is open, can compel attendance and documents, and publishes findings, so it establishes facts others cannot. The view that it is just a select committee ignores those powers.
questions.hint: Open, compulsory and published.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Compare the safeguards in recall and impeachment.
questions.stem: Compare the safeguard built into a recall referendum with the safeguard built into impeachment, and say which offers the better protection against a wrong removal.

answer.exemplar: Both procedures protect against wrongful removal, but they protect different interests and in different ways. The recall referendum protects the public against a bad official, because the voters can end the term without proving misconduct and without waiting for a legal case; its weakness is that it is blunt, since a candidate can be removed by a temporary wave of dissatisfaction. The impeachment procedure protects the official, because it requires a fixed day, a threshold of support, a public hearing of evidence and a supermajority vote, so that no removal happens on the strength of an allegation alone; its weakness is that it may be too slow when the harm is continuing. The impeachment safeguards are the better protection against a wrong removal, because a recall cannot test whether the complaint was true, only whether enough people were annoyed.

questions.explanation: Impeachment tests the evidence; a recall tests only how many are dissatisfied. The claim that a popular vote is surest ignores that it cannot test the case.
questions.hint: One procedure tests facts, the other tests mood.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain how question time operates.
questions.stem: Describe how question time works in our council, including what happens to a question that cannot be answered on the day.

answer.exemplar: Question time is a fixed part of each sitting set aside for questions to the minister responsible for the portfolio under discussion. Members table their questions in advance so that the minister can prepare, and the minister answers orally in the chamber, where members may pursue the answer with a short supplementary question. Questions are limited in number and in length so that a single member cannot consume the period, and the order in which members are called is governed by a rota that gives opposition members a share of the time. Where a minister cannot answer on the day, the answer is promised in writing and circulated to all members within a stated period, and the question remains open until the written answer has been laid before the council.

questions.explanation: Question time is prepared and time-limited, with a rota for the call and unanswered questions going to writing. The idea that questions may come at any point undercuts the preparation.
questions.hint: Tabled, timed, and sometimes answered in writing.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Set out the impeachment stages and their purpose.
questions.stem: Set out the stages of the impeachment procedure as we apply them, and explain what each stage is for.

answer.exemplar: Our procedure runs in four stages and each one filters out error. First the complaint: a member must collect signatures from a set proportion of the guild, and that threshold is the first check, because a bare accusation from one member should never be enough to put an officer on trial. Second the committee: once a complaint is carried, a committee is appointed to examine the evidence, take statements, and decide whether a prima facie case exists. Third the fixed-day debate: if the committee reports a case, the guild sets aside a day, at least a fortnight ahead, so that the accused knows the case and can prepare. Fourth the decision: only then may the guild resolve on removal, and the vote carries the two thirds threshold. The stages exist so that each kind of error is caught by a different one.

questions.explanation: Complaint, committee, fixed-day debate and decision each filter a different kind of error, so skipping a stage removes a check. The belief that the committee alone can decide discards the final vote.
questions.hint: Four stages, each filtering something.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Weigh the protective and shielding effects of a threshold.
questions.stem: Explain how the impeachment threshold protects the guild, and how the same threshold can let a guilty officer stay in office.

answer.exemplar: A high threshold protects the guild in two ways. It keeps the removal power away from a temporary coalition of grievance, so an officer is not dismissed because a particular week was angry, and it keeps the assembly from using the impeachment route as an alternative way of settling ordinary political arguments. The same threshold works against the guild in the mirror image. If the majority that would bring a serious complaint is itself divided, or if the officers who would enforce the removal are among those protected, then the standard that was set to prevent rash removals becomes a shield for the conduct it was meant to expose. The threshold therefore has to be read with the other safeguards: the complaint stage, the committee evidence, the fixed day and the published record. Without them, a high bar is not protection but concealment.

questions.explanation: A high threshold prevents rash and political removals but can protect a guilty officer, so it works only alongside the other safeguards. The belief that a high bar is always protective ignores what it shelters.
questions.hint: Read the threshold with the other safeguards.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why neutrality is required of a ceremonial head.
questions.stem: Explain why a ceremonial head of state is normally chosen for neutrality rather than for political strength, and note the danger that lies in the role.

answer.exemplar: A ceremonial head is chosen for neutrality because the role's value lies in being a constitutional point of continuity that no faction can claim. If the office were filled by a partisan with a following, the same figure who signs the declarations in a calm week would be suspected of shaping events in a turbulent one, and the assembly's own authority would be hollowed out by the shadow of a rival. The danger lies in the difficulty of the role for someone who does nothing. A ceremonial head who never speaks may be written off as a decoration, which is a poor outcome, because the office then supplies no reassurance at all; a ceremonial head who speaks often becomes a second voice competing with the council, which is a worse one. The successful holder therefore signs without protest, counsels privately, and speaks rarely and only where the constitution allows.

questions.explanation: Neutrality makes the office useful, because continuity must belong to no faction. The dangerous failure is not silence but competing with the council, which revives the factionalism neutrality excludes.
questions.hint: Continuity must belong to no faction.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain how qualification changes spending control.
questions.stem: Explain how qualified appropriations change the way the council controls spending, and set out the risks that they create.

answer.exemplar: A qualified appropriation changes the council's control by splitting the decision in two. With an ordinary payment the council decides once, at the point of authorisation, and thereafter the officers have a blank cheque for the stated sum. With a qualified payment the council decides twice: once on the purpose and the sum, and again when the condition is tested, and if the condition fails the money is simply never released. That second decision is where the control lies, and it is a control the council could not have exercised from the outset because it does not yet know how the work will go. The risks are real. A condition that is vague cannot be applied and becomes a rhetorical flourish. A condition whose certifying body is dissolved leaves the payment stranded. A condition that is too strict delays work that must be done, and the delay itself causes harm where a hive cannot be fed on time.

questions.explanation: Qualification splits the decision so the council can refuse money when a condition fails, but vague conditions strand payments. The claim that conditions are administrative ignores the second decision.
questions.hint: Two decisions instead of one.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish pardon, remission and commutation.
questions.stem: Set out the differences between a pardon, a remission of sentence and a commutation, and give an example of each.

answer.exemplar: A pardon forgives the offence itself, so that the person is treated as if it had never been committed, and it removes the stigma as well as the penalty; it is the appropriate answer to a conviction that was wrong. A remission of sentence reduces the term that remains to be served without touching the conviction, so the record of the offence stays but the time is shortened; it answers a sentence that was lawful but unduly severe for the individual. A commutation changes the form of the punishment while leaving the fact of guilt and the proportionality of the sentence intact, as when imprisonment is replaced by a fine or by community service. The three differ in what they leave behind, which is why choosing between them is a question about what must be cured.

questions.explanation: A pardon forgives the offence, a remission shortens the term and a commutation changes the penalty's form, each leaving something behind. Confusing remission with pardon ignores that the conviction remains.
questions.hint: Ask what each one leaves behind.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Weigh the case for holding a public inquiry.
questions.stem: Weigh the case for and against holding a public inquiry into a disputed episode, and give me a conclusion for the log.

answer.exemplar: The case for an inquiry is that a dispute which cannot be settled by argument tends to poison the guild's working relations, and an inquiry which publishes its findings gives both sides a common set of facts to argue about. It also protects the officers concerned, because a proper procedure with compulsory powers and a public record establishes that they were examined fairly, which an accusation never does. The case against is that an inquiry takes months, costs the guild a great deal, and produces findings that few read, while the political conflict it was meant to settle simply moves to the next occasion. Its worst feature is the temptation to choose a form of inquiry that is bound to reach the conclusion the guild wants. An inquiry is worth holding when the facts are genuinely contested and public trust is at stake, but the terms should be settled before any members are appointed.

questions.explanation: An inquiry is worth holding where facts are contested and trust damaged, if the terms are fixed in advance. The assumption that any inquiry settles disputes ignores that a badly framed one relocates it.
questions.hint: Fix the terms before appointing anyone.

questions.learningObjective: Explain the signature threshold for a recall.
questions.stem: Explain why a recall referendum is generally designed to need a signature threshold as well as a majority at the poll.

answer.exemplar: The signature threshold exists to filter out two things before any voter goes to the polls. The first is frivolousness: without a minimum number of signatures, an enthusiastic minority could put a question to the whole membership at negligible cost, and the campaign would shift from a serious question about an official's conduct to a contest of who can mobilise the most noise. The second is purpose: the signature requirement is the moment at which the proponents must show that the issue is serious enough to divide the membership, and it gives the council a formal basis for fixing the date and the question rather than reacting to a petition signed in a weekend. The majority at the poll then answers a different question, which is whether a sufficient share of the membership actually wants the change. Setting both means that recall needs both a serious beginning and a broad ending.

questions.explanation: The signature threshold filters frivolous campaigns and shows seriousness, while the poll majority shows broad support, so both must be met. The complaint about bureaucracy ignores the cost of a poll.
questions.hint: Serious at the start, broad at the end.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: State the conditions attached to granting clemency.

stimulus.body: Extract from the guild warrant for clemency: the power to grant pardon, remission or commutation shall be exercised only upon a recommendation of the courts, and only for reasons that can be stated in writing and published; the reasons and the recommendation shall be laid before the guild within fourteen days of the grant.

questions.stem: Under the warrant, which condition attaches to the granting of clemency?

options.text: That the grant must be approved by a two thirds vote of the guild before it takes effect.
options.misconception: invents a vote requirement the warrant does not impose

options.text: That the grant may be made only during the ceremonial head's annual address to the guild.
options.misconception: restricts clemency to a single annual occasion

options.text: That written reasons must be stated and published, and the recommendation laid before the guild.
That the grant may be made only where the offence has been pardoned by another authority.
options.misconception: invents a prior foreign pardon as a precondition

questions.explanation: The warrant requires published written reasons and a judicial recommendation laid before the guild, a condition about justification not a vote. A two thirds approval would put clemency in the council's hands.
questions.hint: Reasons published, recommendation laid.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Interpret the pattern of ceremonial activity.
questions.stem: Ceremonial activity by type: 84 declarations signed, 26 foreign delegations received, 9 public remarks made, and 4 occasions where the head declined to attend. What do these figures suggest about the role?

options.text: The head of state spends most of its time on formal acts, since 84 declarations dominate the count.
options.misconception: treats one category's size as a measure of the whole role

options.text: The head of state is too active in public life, since 9 public remarks exceed the 4 absences.
options.misconception: compares remarks with absences as if they were alike

options.text: The head of state has little to do, since only 123 formal acts were recorded across the year.
options.misconception: asserts a low total without noticing the 123 figure is high

options.text: The role is dominated by formal acts, with public speaking rare and absences rare, which fits a ceremonial description.

questions.explanation: Formal acts outnumber public speaking more than nine to one, which fits a ceremonial rather than a political description. Comparing remarks with absences treats different events as comparable.
questions.hint: Separate formal acts from public speech.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Assess question time as a check on the executive.
questions.stem: Assess question time as a check on the executive, and set out what would make it a stronger check.

answer.exemplar: Question time is a real check, though a modest one. It makes the minister account for his portfolio in public, on the record, in front of the members who will judge him at the next election, and it means that a failure to answer does not pass unremarked. It also disciplines the whole chamber, because the minister must be prepared to know his brief, and the questions put by members must be relevant or they will be ruled out of order. Its weaknesses are equally plain. The minister controls the answers and the framing, and answers given orally can be ingenious without being complete. The number of questions is small compared with the volume of the portfolio, so the session samples the work rather than examining it. The most effective improvements do not add more time but make the answers bind: requiring the principal answer to be given in writing and published, so that it can be quoted and checked.

questions.explanation: Question time makes the minister account in public on the record, but it samples rather than examines and the minister controls the answers. More minutes do not fix how hard a spoken answer is to check.
questions.hint: Make the answers bind, not longer.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify the principal safeguard in a public inquiry.
questions.stem: What is the most important safeguard built into a public committee of inquiry of this kind?

options.text: That the inquiry must report within a fixed number of sitting days after its first sitting.
options.misconception: treats a reporting deadline as the principal safeguard

options.text: That the terms of reference are settled and published before the inquiry begins sitting.
That the chair of the inquiry is chosen by a vote of the guild membership at large.
options.misconception: assumes the choice of chair is a prescribed safeguard

options.text: That the inquiry must be chaired by a member of the opposition where one exists.
options.misconception: invents a requirement about who may chair an inquiry

questions.explanation: Settling and publishing the terms first removes the temptation to shape an inquiry to a preferred conclusion, the safeguard that matters most. The alternatives are administrative only.
questions.hint: Fix the question before the hearing starts.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the unconditional share of a vote.
questions.stem: Budget profile: the guild's annual feed vote is 12,000 marks, of which 5,000 is released without condition, 4,000 is released on the storekeeper's certificate, and 3,000 is released only after an inspector's report is laid before the council. What percentage of the feed vote is released unconditionally?
questions.explanation: 5,000 of 12,000 is 41.67 per cent, since 5,000 divided by 12,000 gives 0.4167. The figure of 7,000 is the conditionally released share rather than the unconditional one.
questions.hint: Divide the unconditional share by the whole vote.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: State the initiating threshold for impeachment.

stimulus.body: Extract from the guild's standing orders: proceedings for the removal of an officer shall not be initiated unless a complaint is carried by not fewer than one tenth of the members of the guild; a complaint so carried shall be referred to a committee of inquiry, whose report shall be laid before the guild, and only upon that report may the guild proceed to the question of removal.

questions.stem: Under the standing orders, what is the minimum number of members needed to initiate removal proceedings?

options.text: None at all, since any member may raise the matter in debate at any ordinary sitting.
options.misconception: assumes removal proceedings can start by a single speech

options.text: A simple majority of the guild, since that is what the final vote on removal requires.
options.misconception: confuses the initiating threshold with the final vote

options.text: Two thirds of the guild, since removal is the gravest power the guild holds.
options.misconception: borrows the removal threshold for the initiating stage

options.text: One tenth of the members, since a complaint must be carried to begin the process.

questions.explanation: The orders require a complaint carried by one tenth of the members to start the process, a lower bar than the eventual vote. The use of the two thirds threshold ignores that it applies at the end.
questions.hint: One tenth starts it; two thirds ends it.
